dossier.notes:
# tauri
## Notes
- A toolkit for small desktop apps whose UI is a web page in the system webview and whose core is Rust. [d1]
## Versions
- Tauri 2 | 2 [d1]
## Setup
- Tauri 2 on linux | Install Rust with rustup, the webkit2gtk and build packages, then npm create tauri-app@latest [d1]
- Tauri 2 on macos | Install Rust with rustup and the Xcode command line tools, then npm create tauri-app@latest [d1]
- Tauri 2 on windows | Install Rust with rustup and the Microsoft C++ build tools (WebView2 ships with Windows 11), then npm create tauri-app@latest [d1]

# sqlite
## Notes
- A SQL database stored in a single file, embedded in the program rather than run as a server. [d2]
## Versions
- SQLite | 3 [d2]
## Setup
- SQLite on linux | sudo apt install sqlite3 [d2]
- SQLite on macos | brew install sqlite [d2]
- SQLite on windows | winget install SQLite.SQLite [d2]

brief.summary: A small Tauri 2 notes app: a web UI in the system webview, a Rust core holding all note logic, SQLite for storage, and the Tauri bundler for installers. Business logic stays in core/ and the UI calls only what commands.rs declares.

layers.name: Tauri 2
layers.whatItIs: A toolkit for small desktop apps whose UI is a web page in the system webview and whose core is Rust.
layers.roleHere: Draws the notes window: note list, editor and search box, as a web page.
layers.whyChosen: You named Tauri. It gives much smaller installers than Electron and a more explicit IPC surface than a plain webview wrapper.
pros: One bundler for all three OSes
cons: Core is Rust, a second language
layers.learnerCost: Basic Tauri project layout, plus enough HTML/JS for the UI and enough Rust for the core.

alternatives.name: Electron
alternatives.pickWhen: You want zero Rust and identical rendering on every OS.

assumptions: The UI is plain web tech (TypeScript, no heavy framework) that you can change.
You are comfortable with some web basics.

layers.name: Rust core behind a thin web UI
layers.whatItIs: The app is split so all logic lives in a Rust library and the UI only shows results and sends requests.
layers.roleHere: core/ holds note create, edit, search and delete rules with no Tauri imports, so it is tested without a window.
layers.whyChosen: A UI-free core is required and is easy to test. It beats keeping logic in JavaScript, which would blur the line between UI and rules.
cons: More files than a single-script app
layers.learnerCost: Rust modules and crates, structs, Result error handling, and serde for converting data to JSON.

alternatives.name: Logic in the JavaScript frontend
cons: Harder to test without a webview
alternatives.pickWhen: You want to avoid Rust entirely.

assumptions: You accept writing the core in Rust, since Tauri requires it.

layers.name: Tauri commands and capabilities
layers.whatItIs: Named Rust functions the web page can call, with a permission list saying what it may call.
layers.roleHere: All calls like list_notes, save_note and delete_note are declared in one commands.rs file, and capabilities grant the UI only those.
layers.whyChosen: It is Tauri's built-in security model, so no extra library is needed. It beats raw custom protocols, which have no permission model.
cons: Every new feature needs a command and a permission
layers.learnerCost: The #[tauri::command] attribute, invoke from JS, and capability JSON files.

alternatives.name: Tauri events only
alternatives.pickWhen: The core must push updates to the UI.

assumptions: The UI uses no filesystem or shell plugins directly.

layers.name: SQLite
layers.whatItIs: A SQL database stored in a single file, embedded in the program rather than run as a server.
layers.roleHere: Stores notes in one database file in the app-data directory, accessed only by the Rust core.
layers.whyChosen: Search, ordering and transactions come built in. That beats plain files, where you write search and safe saving yourself.
layers.learnerCost: Basic SQL, a simple migration step, and a Rust SQLite crate.

alternatives.name: Markdown files in app-data
alternatives.pickWhen: Notes must be editable in other editors.

assumptions: Notes are text only, with no sync between devices.

layers.name: Tauri dialog plugin
layers.whatItIs: An official add-on that opens native file dialogs from the app.
layers.roleHere: Lets the user export a note to a file or import one with the system file picker.
layers.whyChosen: It is the official route and works through capabilities. It beats a browser file input, which cannot choose a save location.
layers.learnerCost: Installing a plugin and granting its permission.
assumptions: Import and export is wanted; tray and shortcuts are left out.

layers.name: Tauri bundler
layers.whatItIs: The Tauri build step that packages the app into an installer for each OS.
layers.roleHere: Runs tauri build to produce a real installer, such as MSI, DMG or deb/AppImage, as the final artifact.
layers.whyChosen: It is built in, with no setup beyond config. Third-party packagers would add steps for no gain.
cons: Builds only for the host OS
layers.learnerCost: Fields in tauri.conf.json such as app name, identifier and icons.

alternatives.name: Plain release binary
alternatives.pickWhen: The app is only for yourself.

assumptions: You build on your own OS; cross-OS builds need CI.

layers.name: No auto-update (manual reinstall)
layers.whatItIs: New versions are shipped by building and installing a fresh installer.
layers.roleHere: Keeps the first release simple: users reinstall to update.
layers.whyChosen: Auto-update needs signing keys and a hosted manifest. For a learner project that costs more than it gives.
layers.learnerCost: None beyond bumping the version number.

alternatives.name: Tauri updater plugin
alternatives.pickWhen: You plan to distribute to real users.

assumptions: The app is not publicly distributed yet.

layers.name: cargo test on the core, plus contract checks
layers.whatItIs: Rust's built-in test runner, run against the UI-free core.
layers.roleHere: Unit-tests note logic against an in-memory SQLite, and checks that every command the UI calls is declared in commands.rs.
layers.whyChosen: Cargo ships it, so no new tool is needed. It beats end-to-end UI tests, which are slow and need a window.
cons: Does not test the real webview
Contract check needs a small script
layers.learnerCost: Writing #[test] functions and using in-memory databases.
assumptions: Manual checks cover the UI itself.

flows.label: packages UI and core into installer

brief.howItFitsTogether: You type a note and press save, so the web UI calls invoke('save_note'). Tauri checks that the capabilities allow it and runs the matching function in commands.rs. That function calls the core, which validates the note and writes it to the SQLite file in app-data. The result returns as JSON and the UI refreshes the list. The bundler later packs the built UI and Rust core into an installer.
risks: Rust's borrow checker slows a web developer at first
Webview rendering differs across operating systems
Missing capability entries make commands fail silently
Linux builds need the right webkit2gtk packages
friction: Tauri's core is Rust, a second language for a web developer; keeping it small limits the cost.
The browser can check only the web UI as a plain page; commands, SQLite, testing and packaging need the command line.
